 1                   I.     INTRODUCTION AND QUALIFICATIONS

 2   Q1.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A.    My name is Steven A. Sierra. My business address is 100 N. Stanton Street,

 5

 6   Q2.   HOW ARE YOU EMPLOYED?

 7   A.    I am employed by El Paso Electric Company ("EPE" or the "Company") as Director

 8         of Financial Accounting.

 9

10   Q3.   HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY SUBMITTED TESTIMONY IN THIS CASE?

11   A.    Yes. I submitted Direct Testimony on August 6, 2026, in support of EPE’s

12         Amended Application for Revision of its Retail Electric Rates (“Amended Filing”).

13

14   Q4.   ARE YOU SPONSORING ANY EXHIBITS IN THIS FILING?

15   A.    Yes. I am sponsoring Exhibits SAS-1R through SAS-11R, which are listed in the

18                    II.   PURPOSE OF REBUTTAL TESTIMONY

19   Q5.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?




                                               1
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1   A.   My rebuttal testimony has two purposes. First, I present EPE's revised Total

 2        Company revenue requirement request, as shown on Exhibit SAS-1R which

 3        reflects the adjustments EPE has agreed to make in rebuttal.

 4               Adjustments to cost of service not specifically discussed in my testimony

 5        are addressed by the corresponding witnesses as listed on Exhibit SAS-2R. Exhibit

 6        SAS-2R also shows the flow through effects of adjustments on cost of service.

 7               Second, I respond to the Direct Testimony of three witnesses: (i) City of

 8        Las Cruces and Doña Ana County ("CLC/DAC") witness Mark Garrett on the

 9        issues of the Company's requested Short Term Incentive Plan (“STIP”) and payroll

10        expenses and their related impact on payroll tax expense, and the recommended

11        disallowances of membership dues and advertising expenses; (ii) New Mexico

12        Public Regulation Commission (“NMPRC” or “Commission”) Advisory Staff

13        (“Staff”) witness Jonah Mauldin on the issue of 60/40 split of customer and

14        Company sharing of non-financial STIP costs; and (iii) Staff witness Naomi

15        Velasquez on the recommended disallowances of membership dues and advertising

16        expenses.

17

                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1                III. RESPONSE TO CLC/DAC WITNESS GARRETT

 2                                  RECOMMENDATIONS

 3   Q6.   WHAT          ARE        CLC/DAC           WITNESS           M.       GARRETT’S

 4         RECOMMENDATIONS REGARDING STIP COSTS REQUESTED BY

 5         THE COMPANY?

 6   A.    CLC/DAC witness Mark Garrett recommends that all STIP costs be excluded from

 7         EPE’s revenue requirement. He relies on the STIP’s financial earnings threshold

 8         and argues that this performance requirement makes the entire STIP a financially

 9         based incentive. Mr. M. Garrett argues that the operational measures principally

10         benefit shareholders or concern activities that EPE is already obligated to perform.

11         He also argues that this structure “shifts shareholder risk to ratepayers” (M. Garrett

12         Direct at 42, lines 7-8) and “rewards employees and shareholders when financial

13         targets are achieved but exposes ratepayers to the cost regardless of actual

14         performance” (M. Garrett Direct at 41, lines 1-2).

15

16   Q7.   DO YOU AGREE WITH MR. M. GARRETT’S PROPOSED ADJUSTMENT

17         TO     REMOVE         ALL      STIP       COSTS      FROM       THE      REVENUE

18         REQUIREMENT?

19   A.    No. The Company’s request for STIP costs in this case follows the Commission's

20         rate treatment established in Case No. 15-00127-UT (“2015 Rate Case”) and again

21         followed in Case No. 20-00104-UT (“2020 Rate Case”). Specifically, the Final
                                                 3
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1         Order in the 2015 Rate Case notes that “due to the variability of the historical data,

 2         EPE should be allowed to recover based upon a three-year historical average of

 3         STIP payouts, and those should be limited to payouts that are not based upon

 4         financial performance” (2015 Rate Case Final Order ¶ 204). Notably, the

 5         Commission’s adoption of this three-year, non-financial approach in the 2015 Rate

 6         Case followed a recommendation made by Doña Ana County itself in that

 7         proceeding (2015 Rate Case Final Order ¶ 210). CLC/DAC now asks the

 8         Commission to abandon the very approach that Doña Ana County advocated and

 9         the Commission adopted, without identifying any change in EPE’s STIP or in

10         circumstances that would justify doing so.

11                The 100% disallowance of EPE’s STIP expense as recommended by

12         CLC/DAC witness M. Garrett should also be rejected as contrary to the

13         Commission’s prior decisions permitting recovery of incentive compensation

14         amounts tied to workgroup performance targets that benefit ratepayers.

15

16   Q8.   WHY IS THE STIP A REASONABLE COST OF PROVIDING SERVICE?

17   A.    EPE’s STIP is part of its overall compensation strategy, which helps to ensure EPE

18         is attracting and retaining the talent it needs in a complex operational and service

19         delivery business model. EPE’s STIP is specifically designed to motivate and

20         reward employees to achieve benefits for customers through reliability and

21         customer service that are consistent with EPE's public service mandate to provide
                                                 4
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1         reliable and cost-effective electrical service, while also bringing employee total

 2         cash compensation closer to market-based levels (Sierra Direct at Q54). As

 3         discussed in my direct testimony, and later again in this testimony, the market

 4         compensation study issued by Mercer in December 2024, which covered 530

 5         exempt non-union employees, concluded that total cash compensation (i.e., base

 6         salary and incentive compensation) for EPE employees is most closely aligned with

 7         the 25th percentile of market. In other words, EPE's overall total cash compensation

 8         is commensurate with the lowest quarter percentile of comparable companies

 9         (Sierra Direct at Q51 and Q52).

10

11   Q9.   DOES     THE     STIP’S     FINANCIAL        THRESHOLD         PERFORMANCE

12         REQUIREMENT MAKE THE ENTIRE STIP A FINANCIALLY BASED

13         INCENTIVE, AS MR. M. GARRETT CLAIMS?

14   A.    No. To clarify, EPE is not seeking recovery of any financially based incentives.

15         Consistent with established Commission policy, EPE removed all incentive

16         compensation tied to financial goals from its request.

17                Mr. M. Garrett’s argument confuses a funding threshold with a performance

18         metric. The financial earnings threshold determines only whether there are enough

19         earnings to fund any award at all. It does not determine what employees must do to

20         earn an award. What employees must actually achieve are the operational metrics

21         (reliability, generating-unit availability, and customer service) to which the plan
                                                5
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1        assigns specific weights. A threshold that governs whether the plan is funded does

 2        not convert those operational metrics into financial ones.

 3               Because the STIP is designed to be self-funded, the financial threshold

 4        simply confirms that EPE’s financial performance in a given plan year is sufficient

 5        to support the payout of the cash award. Moreover, the 2025 Annual Cash Bonus

 6        Plan language that Mr. M. Garrett cites states that “no plan payout will be made

 7        unless EPE achieves the non-GAAP EBITDA of at least threshold unless the People

 8        and Remuneration Committee (“PARCO”) of the Board of Directors of EPE

 9        determines otherwise” (Exhibit MEG-3, page 11 of 56). The threshold is therefore

10        not even an absolute condition; the PARCO retains discretion to award a STIP

11        based on the circumstances of the plan year.

12

13   Q10. DOES EPE’S STIP STRUCTURE EXPOSE CUSTOMERS TO STIP COSTS

14        REGARDLESS OF ACTUAL PERFORMANCE, AS MR. M. GARRETT

15        CLAIMS?

16   A.   No. Mr. M. Garrett argues that “employees may receive significant payouts when

17        financial targets are met, yet ratepayers fund the base incentive expense embedded

18        in rates even if those targets are not achieved” (M. Garrett Direct at 41, lines 3-4).

19        The facts show the opposite, for three reasons.

20               First, the amount in rates is capped. Because the STIP amount embedded in

21        rates excludes all costs related to financial metrics, any “significant payout” above
                                                6
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1        that level is funded by shareholders, not customers. The better EPE performs, the

 2        larger the share of the payout borne by shareholders.

 3                 Second, the concern that customers will pay for awards that are never made

 4        is unfounded in practice. EPE has paid a STIP every year going back at least 20

 5        years.

 6                 Third, the three-year average the Commission adopted in the 2015 Rate

 7        Case, and that was followed in the 2020 Rate Case, is specifically designed to

 8        smooth year-to-year fluctuations in STIP payouts, so that the amount in rates

 9        reflects a normalized level rather than a single unusually high or low year.

10

11   Q11. DO YOU AGREE WITH MR. M. GARRETT’S ARGUMENT THAT THE

12        OPERATIONAL            (NON-FINANCIAL)          METRICS        OF     THE      STIP

13        REPRESENT ACTIVITIES ALREADY REQUIRED OF A REGULATED

14        ELECTRIC UTILITY, AND THEREFORE ARE NOT DEMONSTRATED

15        TO BE INCREMENTALLY BENEFICIAL TO CUSTOMERS?

16   A.   No. The existence of a utility service obligation does not mean all levels of

17        operational performance are the same. EPE’s STIP establishes measurable

18        objectives for reliability (SAIDI, SAIFI, and generation Equivalent Availability

19        Factor) and customer service. EPE's STIP program is designed based on the

20        assumption that EPE will achieve its non-financial goals at the target level. These

21        operational targets in the STIP are typically designed as "stretch" goals. This means
                                               7
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1        the target levels for these metrics are generally designed to be equal to or

 2        improvements over the average of recent years’ results. This design motivates

 3        employees towards continual improvement, specifically in the operational areas of

 4        reliability and customer service, which directly benefits customers by aligning the

 5        interests of employees with the interests of customers in these operational areas.

 6

 7   Q12. WHAT ARE MR. M. GARRETT’S RECOMMENDATIONS REGARDING

 8        THE PAYROLL ADJUSTMENT REQUESTED BY THE COMPANY?

 9   A.   Mr. M. Garrett recommends that no escalation should be applied to non-union

10        employee salaries, and that the base year expense ratio, rather than a three-year

11        average, be used to calculate the adjusted payroll expense.

12

13   Q13. DO YOU AGREE WITH MR. M. GARRETT’S RECOMMENDATION

14        THAT NO ESCALATION RATE SHOULD BE APPLIED TO NON-UNION

15        SALARIES?

16   A.   No. Mr. M. Garrett argues that EPE did not provide adequate justification or

17        rationale for the proposed non-union escalation. The interrogatories referenced in

18        CLC/DAC witness M. Garrett’s testimony did not include EPE’s response to Doña

19        Ana County’s Interrogatory DAC 1-19, which is attached to this testimony as

20        Exhibit SAS-07R, where EPE provided its policy regarding pay increases including

21        the guiding principles which are used to ensure a consistent approach to distributing
                                               8
                            EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                            REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1   merit increases. That response, which was made available to Mr. M. Garrett,

 2   provides the additional explanation that he claims is lacking.

 3          CLC/DAC witness M. Garrett also argues that using a three-year average

 4   for non-union wage increases to support the request in this case is inappropriate

 5   because the average includes the “unusually high inflationary period from 2022

 6   through 2024” (M. Garrett Direct at 45, lines 5-8). EPE’s response to Staff’s

 7   Interrogatory Staff 2-54, which is attached to this testimony as Exhibit SAS-08R,

 8   includes a listing of EPE’s non-union merit increases back to the 2020 base year,

 9   which precedes the high inflationary period referenced by CLC/DAC witness M.

10   Garrett, and shows that EPE’s level of non-union merit increases has been steady.

11   In other words, EPE’s merit increases are not based on or tied to inflation, and are

12   instead intended to, among other things as noted in EPE’s response to DAC 1-19

13   (Exhibit SAS-07R), maintain moderate pay growth for contributor-level performers

14   near market. As noted earlier in my testimony, the Company's most recent market

15   compensation study concluded that total cash compensation (salary plus incentive

16   compensation) for EPE non-union employees is most closely aligned with the 25th

17   percentile of market or comparable companies, or well below market for similarly

18   situated jobs both in the electric utility industry and the job market as a whole.

19          Lastly, as noted in Q55 of my Direct Testimony and in EPE’s response to

20   DAC 1-20, which is attached to this testimony as Exhibit SAS-0f9R, the actual


                                           9
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1        average merit increase awarded to non-union employees in February 2026 matches

 2        the timing and the amount (4.0%) included in the Company’s payroll adjustment.

 3

 4   Q14. PLEASE EXPLAIN MR. M. GARRETT’S ARGUMENT REGARDING THE

 5        EXPENSE RATIO USED TO CALCULATE THE ADJUSTED PAYROLL

 6        EXPENSE.

 7   A.   Mr. M. Garrett argues that EPE’s historical expense ratios have been declining,

 8        indicating a trend, and that the most recent base year expense ratio provides a more

 9        reasonable estimate of future expense levels than a multi-year average (M. Garrett

10        Direct at 45, lines 9-12).

11

12   Q15. DO YOU AGREE WITH MR. M. GARRETT’S ARGUMENT USING THE

13        BASE YEAR PAYROLL EXPENSE RATIO, RATHER THAN A THREE-

14        YEAR AVERAGE?

15   A.   No. Like the three-year average used to calculate EPE’s STIP request, the use of a

16        three-year average payroll expense ratio, as approved by the Commission in EPE’s

17        2015 Rate Case and followed by EPE in the 2020 Rate Case, serves to mitigate the

18        risk of significant fluctuations in the ratio and provides a normalized measure of

19        payroll expected to be charged to operations and maintenance (“O&M”) expense.

20        Further, using a Base Period expense ratio is not necessarily a more reasonable

21        indication of future expense levels, as CLC/DAC witness M. Garrett contends. In
                                              10
                            EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                            REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1   fact, for January 2026 – September 2026, the expense ratio for EPE’s total payroll

 2   was approximately 62%, which is higher than any of the expense ratios used in

 3   EPE’s payroll adjustment in this case, and higher than the Base Period ratio that

 4   CLC/DAC witness M. Garrett is recommending.

 5           Mr. M. Garrett’s testimony also notes that EPE did not recognize offsetting

 6   factors, including employee turnover and productivity improvements (M. Garrett

 7   Direct at 45, lines 13-15). Because EPE’s payroll expense in this case is based on

 8   an actual headcount of 1,229 employees as of the end of the Base Period (September

 9   30, 2025), there is already a measure of vacancy included in the requested payroll

10   adjustment since any open positions at that time would not have been included in

11   the calculation. In fact, EPE’s headcount as of September 30, 2026 was 1,251

12   employees, so headcount has increased in the year since the end of the Base Period

13   in this case.

14           Mr. M. Garrett also asserts that EPE’s adjustment fails to recognize

15   productivity improvements. Mr. M. Garrett does not quantify any such productivity

16   offset, and his recommendation therefore rests on an unsupported assumption.

17   Moreover, any productivity effects are already reflected in EPE’s use of actual Base

18   Period headcount and actual payroll, which capture the Company’s realized staffing

19   and output levels rather than a hypothetical projection.

20


                                          11
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1   Q16. DO YOU AGREE WITH MR. M. GARRETT’S ADJUSTMENT TO

 2        PAYROLL TAX EXPENSE?

 3   A.   No. As indicated above, EPE does not agree with CLC/DAC witness Garrett's

 4        proposed adjustments to incentive compensation, payroll expense, or the payroll

 5        expense ratios, therefore there should be no corresponding adjustments to payroll

 6        tax expense.

 7

 8   Q17. PLEASE DESCRIBE MR. M. GARRETT'S PROPOSED ADJUSTMENTS

 9        TO DUES AND MEMBERSHIP EXPENSE?

10   A.   Mr. M. Garrett recommends the disallowance of the Company’s Electric Edison

11        Institute (“EEI”) membership dues in their entirety, as well as the 50% - 50%

12        sharing of costs between customers and shareholders for the Company’s remaining

13        dues and memberships.

14

15   Q18. SHOULD EPE’S EEI DUES BE DISALLOWED IN THEIR ENTIRETY?

16   A.   No. A total disallowance is unnecessary because the portion of EEI dues that could

17        raise a concern, lobbying, is already excluded. Consistent with 17.3.350.11 NMAC,

18        and as confirmed in EPE’s response to DAC 1-40, which is attached to this

19        testimony as Exhibit SAS-10R, EPE records the portions of EEI dues identified as

20        lobbying-related directly to non-operating FERC Account 426.4. That account is

21        excluded entirely from EPE’s cost of service. The same is true of EEI's other
                                              12
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1        advocacy efforts, which are recorded below the line and are not part of EPE's

 2        request.

 3               What remains in cost of service pays for services that Mr. M. Garrett himself

 4        acknowledges EEI provides: policy development, industry research, conferences,

 5        educational programs, communications, and forums through which member

 6        utilities like EPE coordinate on accounting, safety, reliability, regulation,

 7        cybersecurity, and utility operations (M. Garrett Direct at 56, lines 6-9). These

 8        services directly contribute to the professional education and standing of EPE’s

 9        employees, as contemplated by 17.3.350.10(B) NMAC. Mr. M. Garrett offers no

10        basis for disallowing these non-lobbying costs.

11

12   Q19. SHOULD THE COMMISSION REQUIRE A 50/50 SHARING OF EPE’S

13        OTHER DUES AND MEMBERSHIPS?

14   A.   No. In EPE's last New Mexico rate case in which this issue was contested, the 2015

15        Rate Case, the Commission did not adopt a 50/50 sharing for membership dues.

16        Instead, it made organization-specific adjustments based on the evidence and the

17        extent to which lobbying, public affairs, media relations, or other advocacy

18        activities were identified. Mr. M. Garrett's across-the-board split ignores that

19        targeted approach.

20               EPE applied the Commission's approach in this case. In Workpaper A-3,

21        Adjustment No. 11 – Membership Dues, EPE separately identified and removed
                                              13
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1        membership and dues costs related to sponsorships, lobbying, and advocacy. The

 2        remaining dues are listed and described individually on pages 4-7 of that workpaper

 3        to show that each contributes to the education and professional standing of EPE’s

 4        employees under 17.3.350.10(B) NMAC. Those dues should be fully recovered,

 5        except for the two chamber of commerce adjustments EPE accepts in response to

 6        Staff witness Velasquez, discussed further below.

 7

 8   Q20. WHAT IS MR. M. GARRETT'S RECOMMENDATION REGARDING

 9        ADVERTISING EXPENSE?

10   A.   CLC/DAC witness M. Garrett recommends the full disallowance of all directly

11        assigned advertising costs in this case, arguing that EPE failed “to affirmatively

12        show through the presentation of clear and convincing evidence that each

13        expenditure is allowable,” as required by Rule 350 (M. Garrett Direct at 64, lines

14        5-7).

15

16   Q21. DO YOU AGREE WITH CLC/DAC WITNESS M. GARRETT'S

17        PROPOSED ADJUSTMENT TO ADVERTISING EXPENSE?

18   A.   No. As an initial matter, EPE has already excluded from its request the categories

19        of advertising that are not recoverable under Rule 17.3.350. In its direct case, EPE

20        removed $3,175,795 on a total Company basis ($482,967 on a New Mexico

21        jurisdictional basis) of non-allowable advertising, and requests recovery of only
                                              14
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1        $461,268 in directly-assigned New Mexico advertising expense, consisting of

 2        allowable categories such as customer billing and payment education, safety,

 3        energy-conservation, and other informational advertising required or encouraged

 4        by the Commission. EPE maintained and provided copies of each related

 5        advertisement in Workpaper A-3, Adjustment No. 8, as required by Rule 350.9(E).

 6        Mr. M. Garrett's recommendation of a 100% disallowance rests on his

 7        characterization of the retained advertising as image or public-relations material.

 8        That characterization is incorrect as applied to the specific line items EPE actually

 9        requests. Each retained advertisement falls within one or more of the allowable

10        categories identified in Rule 350, and none is designed primarily to promote a

11        favorable public image of the Company. EPE identifies and supports each retained

12        item within its filed request in Workpaper A-3, Adjustment No. 8 – Advertising-

13        Amended Filing, demonstrating that each requested expenditure is an allowable

14        advertising expense under Rule 350.

15

16                 IV. RESPONSE TO STAFF WITNESS MAULDIN

17                                RECOMMENDATIONS

18   Q22. WHAT DOES STAFF WITNESS MAULDIN RECOMMEND REGARDING

19        STIP COSTS REQUESTED BY THE COMPANY?

20   A.   Staff witness Mauldin’s testimony notes that EPE has appropriately excluded the

21        financially based portion of its STIP, consistent with prior Commission orders, and
                                               15
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1        supports recovery of EPE's requested non-financial STIP costs but recommends

 2        that recovery be limited to 60% of the requested amount, with the remaining 40%

 3        borne by the Company's shareholders (Mauldin Direct at 17, lines 2-12).

 4

 5   Q23. WHAT        IS     THE      BASIS        FOR      MR.      MAULDIN’S          60/40

 6        RECOMMENDATION?

 7   A.   Mr. Mauldin reasons that if ratepayers fund the entirety of a STIP, a company

 8        collects those amounts through rates regardless of whether awards are actually paid

 9        out and bears no financial consequence if the program underperforms. He argues

10        that 60/40 sharing gives the company a genuine incentive to ensure the program

11        achieves its stated operational objectives (Mauldin Direct at 17-18).

12

13   Q24. DO YOU AGREE WITH MR. MAULDIN’S 60/40 RECOMMENDATION?

14   A.   No. As discussed in my Direct Testimony and previously in this testimony, EPE is

15        not requesting any financially based incentives in its request and has followed

16        established Commission policy to only request a three-year historical average of the

17        non-financially based portion of the Company's STIP for recovery in this case. The

18        non-financially based portion of the STIP requested in this case represents

19        approximately 44.73% of the total STIP, as calculated and presented on page 9 of

20        Workpaper A-3, Adjustment No. 3 Amended Filing (Salaries and Wages). Staff’s


                                              16
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1        recommendation is to only allow recovery of 60% of the already adjusted 44.73%,

 2        or effectively only about 27% of its total STIP, on a pre-capitalized basis.

 3

 4   Q25. DOES EPE COLLECT STIP COSTS IN RATES WITHOUT REGARD TO

 5        WHETHER AWARDS ARE PAID, AS MR. MAULDIN SUGGESTS?

 6   A.   No. Mr. Mauldin’s premise is a hypothetical in which customers fund the entire

 7        STIP, which is not EPE's request. As I explained in response to Mr. M. Garrett, the

 8        concern is also unfounded in fact: EPE has paid a STIP for at least 20 years. And

 9        the three-year historical average the Commission adopted, and has followed in prior

10        cases, already mitigates the risk of year-to-year fluctuations in payouts.

11

12   Q26. DOES EPE NEED A 40% SHAREHOLDER SHARE TO HAVE A GENUINE

13        INCENTIVE TO MEET ITS STIP OBJECTIVES?

14   A.   No. The incentive Mr. Mauldin seeks already exists. EPE employees are directly

15        incentivized to meet STIP objectives because STIP awards are a key component of

16        their total compensation. The Company, in turn, has a strong incentive to see those

17        goals met. As I noted earlier, even at target-level STIP payouts, total cash

18        compensation for EPE non-union employees is most closely aligned with the 25th

19        percentile of the market. If the Company did not consistently meet its STIP goals

20        and pay incentive compensation, it would risk falling further below market and

21        could find it difficult to attract and retain the personnel it needs. Shifting 40% of
                                                17
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     STEVEN A. SIERRA

 1        these costs to shareholders would not create any incentive that does not already

 2        exist.

 3

DAC 1-19.

      Payroll: Please provide the Company’s policy regarding pay increases, and explain if the
      Company grants general pay increases, if the general pay increases are granted on the same
      date for all qualifying employees, an explanation of the alternative dates if that is used
      instead of a uniform increase date, if the individual increases are based on merit, and the
      different methods are used to determine the amount pay increases for each payroll group
      (contract, management’s decision, etc.).


RESPONSE:

      EPE pay-for-performance philosophy emphasizes recognizing and rewarding employees'
      valuable contributions by paying competitive salaries in a fiscally responsible manner.
      Merit increases for non-union employees are distributed uniformly on the same day, while
      union employees receive increases in accordance with the terms outlined in the Collective
      Bargaining Agreement. The contractual merit increase percentages and dates for the union
      employees can be found in Workpaper A-3, Adjustment No 3, page 5.

      Individual increases for non-union employees are based on merit. Performance evaluations
      are conducted on employees before merit increases are distributed. To reinforce a
      performance-based culture and the use of market-based compensation, the following
      guiding principles are used to ensure a consistent approach to distributing merit increases:

       •     Pay for performance by providing the highest pay increases to top performers;
       •     Lower or unacceptable performers receive minimum or no pay increases;
       •     Accelerate pay for high performers who are low to market;
       •     Maintain moderate pay growth for contributor-level performers near market; and
       •     Decelerate pay growth for contributors at or above market.
